issues.legal_issue: A partition or family settlement of joint ancestral property cannot give a female recipient a share where she had no pre-existing right to that property.
material_facts: The land was part of the father’s ancestral property and remained joint before the disputed partition.
The father allotted the land to his minor daughter under the disputed partition, although she had no pre-existing share in the joint ancestral property.
The daughter sought to evict a tenant on the basis that the partition had made her the landlady.
issues.conclusion: The partition could not make the daughter the landlady of the land, so her eviction claim based on that asserted status was misconceived.
issues.legal_principle: A partition can be made only among persons with pre-existing rights in the property. Under Hindu law, a female has no share in joint ancestral property while it remains joint, though she may receive a share in a husband’s or father’s self-acquired property or in that person’s share after partition of coparcenary property. A family settlement accepted in lieu of partition must reflect legal entitlements and cannot be used to circumvent the law. No earlier case is relied on for this principle.

predicates.eviction_claim_based_on_partition: A claimant sought to evict a tenant by asserting landlady status obtained through a partition or family settlement.
predicates.joint_ancestral_property: The property was ancestral property that remained joint before the arrangement.
predicates.female_recipient_without_preexisting_sha: A female family member received the property under the arrangement despite having no pre-existing share in the joint ancestral property.

issues.definition: When an eviction claim rests on a female recipient’s allotment from joint ancestral property despite her having no pre-existing share, the partition-based claim to landlord status is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A transfer of land, including a partition, cannot give a transferee the right to terminate a protected tenancy that existed before the transfer when the transfer occurred after the applicable cutoff.
material_facts: The tenant was a protected lessee before the land was allotted to the respondent under the 1959 partition.
The respondent sought to terminate the tenancy and evict the tenant after becoming the alleged landlady through that partition.
The 1963 amendment to Section 38(7) included transfers by partition and operated retrospectively.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming the partition was valid, it did not give the respondent the right to terminate the tenant’s pre-existing protected tenancy.
issues.legal_principle: Section 38(7) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, as amended in 1963, provides that a transfer after 1 August 1953, whether by partition or otherwise, does not confer a right to terminate the tenancy of a protected lessee whose protected status arose before the transfer. The amendment is retrospective. No earlier case is relied on for this rule.

predicates.termination_or_eviction_proceeding: A transferee sought to terminate a tenant’s tenancy or recover possession from the tenant.
predicates.transfer_after_applicable_cutoff: The land was transferred after the cutoff applicable to the restriction on termination rights.
predicates.protected_tenancy_predated_transfer: The tenant’s protected status arose before the transfer of the land.

issues.definition: If a transferee seeks termination or eviction after a transfer made beyond the applicable cutoff, and the protected tenancy predates that transfer, the transferee cannot terminate that tenancy.

issues.legal_issue: A protected tenant who remained a tenant until the statutory vesting point became the owner of the land, so a later proceeding to evict the tenant for rent arrears could not succeed.
material_facts: The appellant had been a protected tenant before 1 August 1953 and continued as a tenant until 1 April 1961.
The respondent initiated proceedings in 1962 to evict the appellant for alleged rent arrears.
The respondent’s asserted status as landlady did not alter the appellant’s continued tenancy through the statutory vesting point.
issues.conclusion: The appellant became the statutory owner on 1 April 1961 and was not liable to be evicted as a tenant for rent arrears in the later proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 46 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, a protected tenant who continued as a tenant through 1 April 1961 became the statutory owner from that date. Once ownership vested, proceedings to evict that person on the ground of tenant default could not be brought. No earlier case is relied on for this rule.

predicates.rent_arrears_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought to evict a tenant for alleged rent arrears after the statutory vesting point.
predicates.protected_tenancy_before_qualifying_cuto: The tenant held protected status before the applicable qualifying cutoff.
predicates.tenancy_continued_until_vesting: The person remained a tenant through the statutory point at which ownership vested.

issues.definition: When a protected tenant remains a tenant through the statutory vesting point, a later rent-arrears eviction proceeding cannot treat that person as a tenant liable to eviction.
